title: Predicting player churn in an MMORPG (WoW)
text:
In this blog post we will see how we can predict player churn in World of Warcraft (WoW), a subscription-based MMORPG that was released in 2004. More precisely, we are interested in predicting a player’s behavior in a given month, and decide whether there is a risk that they will stop playing the next month. To do so, we want to train a machine learning model that, given features based on each player and on the overall playerbase, will be able to predict whether player X will stop playing in the month of May 2009 (for example).
Through the post we will build a full machine learning pipeline: we use
polars for dataframe operations; skrub is used for data exploration, feature engineering and constructing the overall execution plan; scikit-learn is imported for the actual ML model; hyperparameter optimization is done using Optuna through skrub’s Data Ops.
To keep the focus of this post on the process rather than the code, most of the lower-level functions will be hidden in collapsible blocks. This includes much of the pre-processing and feature engineering, although important sections will be highlighted as needed.

title: Predicting player churn in an MMORPG (WoW)
text:
1 Modeling player churn
Modeling user churn is a common application of machine learning models, though the definition of churn is typically business’ specific. In general, by “user churn” one refers to “a user that does not come back to the service”. In the context of WoW, user churn would refer to those users that do not come back to the game and suspend their monthly subscription. As we do not have access to the actual subscription data, we assume that each player suspends their subscription as soon as they stop playing for a month.
For this post, we aggregate player behaviors at a monthly basis, and add a has_played flag that tells us if a player has played at during each month.






Important



Our objective
Given a month (e.g., June), we want to use all the data up to the last day of the previous month (all months until May included) to predict whether a user will churn in July (i.e., their has_played flag will be False in July).


The idea is that, by knowing that user X will churn in July, we should be able to use the month of June to apply some incentive to the user so they won’t churn.
One caveat with this modeling strategy is that we are working with historical data, so we cannot actually apply said incentive and observe whether it has an impact like in a typical A/B test.

1.1 Building the churn dataset
We begin by adding two columns to the historical dataset: in the first we store each timestamp, truncated to have a monthly resolution; in the second we track the first month for each character. Additionally, we add a constant has_played column that acts as our “player was seen” flag.
Since we are interested in monthly snapshots, the dataset is then reduced to select only the unique (character, month) pairs.







def make_data(df):
    """
    Add a timestamp column with monthly resolution, the first month for each
    character, and a constant column that acts as flag. 
    """

    data = (
        df.with_columns(
            pl.col("timestamp").dt.truncate("1mo").alias("month"),
            first_month=pl.col("timestamp").dt.truncate("1mo").min().over("char"),
        )
        .unique(subset=["char", "month"])
        .with_columns(pl.lit(True).alias("has_played"))
    )
    return data
data = make_data(df)




Since we want to predict the behavior a player will have over a single month, our target variable will be grouped by “user-month” (e.g., 153_2026-12). However, not all players will play at least once every month, so by relying exclusively on the historical data we would be missing samples; to get around this problem we generate a char_month dataset that contains all unique combinations of users and months by executing the cross-product between the unique users and the range of months.






NoneCross product





The cross product between two sets (in this case, months and unique users) builds a new set where each element in the first set is paired with all elements in the second set.

def make_user_month(df):
    """
    Create a DataFrame with all unique combinations of users and months.
    
    The month range is extracted from the dataset.  
    """

    months = pl.datetime_range(
        start=df.select(pl.col("timestamp").dt.truncate("1mo").min()).collect().item(),
        end=df.select(pl.col("timestamp").dt.truncate("1mo").max()).collect().item(),
        interval="1mo",
        closed="both",
        eager=True,
    )

    char_month = (
        df
        .select("char")
        .unique()
        .join(months.to_frame(name="month").lazy(), how="cross")
    )
    return char_month

Now that we have all the combinations (character, month), we can join back the prepared data to mark all the months in which each character was found online, and marking all others with has_played=False.
Additionally, the resulting rows are filtered to remove all pairs (char, month) whose month precedes the character’s first month. We should not have a row about a character’s playtime in January if they started playing in August!







def add_churn(user_month, data):
    """
    Merge the user-month DataFrame with the actual play data.
    The resulting DataFrame will have a "has_played" column indicating
    whether the user played in that month. Any missing values in "has_played" are
    filled with False: missing values mean that the player did not play in that
    particular month.
    """

    df_with_user_month = (
        user_month.join(
            data,
            on=["char", "month"],
            how="left",
        )
        .with_columns(pl.col("has_played").fill_null(False))
        # Fill missing values in the first_month column with each character's
        # first month
        .with_columns(first_month=pl.col("first_month").min().over("char"))
        # Remove (char, month) rows where the month precedes the character's
        # first month
        .filter(pl.col("first_month") <= pl.col("month"))
        .select(
            "char",
            "month",
            "has_played",
            "first_month",
        )
    )
    return df_with_user_month

Finally, we can put everything together in a single function that takes the historical data as input and returns a dataset with the churn indication as output:

def build_churn_dataset(historical_data):
    # Load the dataset
    data = make_data(historical_data)
    # Add the combinations of user months
    user_month = make_user_month(historical_data)
    churn_data = add_churn(user_month, data)
    return churn_data

In each row, the flag has_played informs us of whether the character logged in at any time in that month, or if they haven’t: this is the target that we want to predict on a monthly basis.

title: Predicting player churn in an MMORPG (WoW)
text:
2 Setting up the ML pipeline
Before starting with feature engineering and actually training the model, it’s worth spending some time understanding the scenario we are in.
The main factor that complicates this scenario is the fact that we are dealing with sequential data points, which are therefore not independent of each other: the position of a player at a time T is strongly correlated with their position at time T+1.

2.1 Building a custom splitter
For this reason, we need to use a splitter that returns sequential splits. A common example of this is scikit-learn’s TimeSeriesSplit. TimeSeriesSplit works by splitting the entire dataset in a given number of splits; during cross-validation, at step K the splitter returns the first k splits as the train split, and the k+1 split as the validation split.

2.1.1 TODO add a diagram here
A downside of TimeSeriesSplit is that the splitter assumes uniformly distributed samples, so that each singular split has the same size as the others. This is a problem for our scenario: our samples are (character, month) pairs, and the number of characters in each month is never constant and indeed increases over time:

For this reason, we need to define a custom splitter that is aware of the constraints we are working with. Given that we are working month-by-month, each split should contain all the characters that played in a specific month, and should be able to do so regardless of the fact that the number of characters changes.
This is what we implement in the following splitter:

from datetime import datetime

# We define the boundaries of the experiment manually
MIN_DATE = datetime.strptime("2008-01-01", "%Y-%m-%d")
MAX_DATE = datetime.strptime("2008-12-30", "%Y-%m-%d")

class Splitter:
    """
    This splitter iterates over the months. It selects all the months up to the 
    split point, which is our cutoff point: it's when we want to perform some 
    operation on users that are marked as "churn risk", i.e., have been predicted
    to churn by the model. 
    """
    def split(self, user_month, has_played=None):
        """
        user_month is our "X", while has_played is the target variable we want 
        to predict
        """
        # has_played is not needed by this splitter, we are only splitting by month
        del has_played
        time_range = pl.date_range(MIN_DATE, MAX_DATE, "1mo", eager=True)
        for split_point in time_range:
            # The test month is the month *after* the split point
            test_month = pl.Series([split_point]).dt.offset_by("1mo").first()
            # Train indices are up to split_point
            # We want a one-month gap
            train_idx = (
                user_month.with_row_index("idx")
                .filter(pl.col("month") <= split_point)["idx"]
                .to_list()
            )
            # Test indices are for the month after split_point
            test_idx = (
                user_month.with_row_index("idx")
                .filter(pl.col("month") == test_month)["idx"]
                .to_list()
            )
            if train_idx and test_idx:
                print(f"Working on month {split_point}")
                yield train_idx, test_idx

    def get_n_splits(self, X, y):
        return sum(1 for _ in self.split(X, y))

Like all other scikit-learn splitters, our splitter is a generator that, given X and y (user_month and has_played in our case), returns the indices of the samples that should be used in each split.

3 Building the pipeline

3.1 Generating the features






NoneFull feature engineering function






# %%
# This function is needed to make sure that we are only ever using historical data
# up to the given month - 1 month. This is to avoid any leakage in the data.
def add_features(X, historical_data, session_gap=30, use_location=True, add_gini=False):
    features_by_month = []

    # Create a session encoder with a 30 minute timeout
    # This encoder is used as a stateless transformer so it is refitted for every
    # month
    session_encoder = SessionEncoder(
        split_by="char", timestamp_col="timestamp", session_gap=session_gap
    )
    historical_data = historical_data.with_columns(
        month=pl.col("timestamp").dt.truncate("1mo")
    )
    last_month = X["month"].max()

    # Grouping by character and zone so that I can get the time spent in each zone
    # Even if users leave the zone, this lets me find how much time a user spends in
    # a given zone
    session_encoder_zone = SessionEncoder(
        split_by=["char", "zone"], timestamp_col="timestamp", session_gap=session_gap
    )
    # Adding fixed features: these features are fixed by character so they don't
    # change over time.
    # historical_data is selected up until the last month because if I select only
    # a single month then any character that did not play in that month will be
    # missing those features
    X = X.join(
        historical_data.filter(pl.col("month") <= last_month)
        .select("char", "race", "charclass")
        .unique("char"),
        on="char",
        how="left",
        maintain_order="left",
    ).with_row_index()  # adding row index so that I can reorder at the end after
    # concatenating
    # kinda defeats the point of using data ops but I think it simplifies the code

    # This is used to add the historical data up to the given month
    # Sorting months is not needed, but forces a consistent order (better for debugging)
    for month in X["month"].unique().sort():
        this_month_X = filter_df_by_month(X, month)

        # Selecting only the entries in the historical data whose month + 2 is equal
        # to the month I am trying to predict on.
        # This means that if the "target month" is April, then the historical data
        # should be filtered to keep only the rows where the current month + 2
        # is equal to April, that is, the month is February. This is equivalent
        # to saying "I want the rows for the current month - 2 months", but it's
        # easier to implement
        kept_historical_data = historical_data.with_columns(
            pl.col("month").dt.offset_by("2mo")
        ).filter(pl.col("month") == month)

        # Session features: a session starts from a heartbeat, then it ends when
        # no more heartbeats are detected for session_gap minutes
        historical_data_with_sessions = session_encoder.fit_transform(
            kept_historical_data
        )
        historical_data_with_sessions = get_session_duration(
            historical_data_with_sessions
        )

        # General features: add session based and playerbase features
        df_with_features = add_general_features(
            this_month_X, historical_data_with_sessions
        )

        # Location features can be useful but take much longer to generate
        if use_location:
            # Zone-session features: a session lasts from the first time a character
            # enters a zone to the moment it leaves it
            # This is useful to get zone-specific features
            historical_data_zone_sessions = session_encoder_zone.fit_transform(
                kept_historical_data
            )
            historical_data_zone_sessions = get_session_duration(
                historical_data_zone_sessions
            )
            df_with_features = add_location_features(
                df_with_features,
                historical_data_zone_sessions,
                add_gini=add_gini,
            )

        features_by_month.append(df_with_features)
        assert len(df_with_features) == len(this_month_X)

    X_res = pl.concat(features_by_month, how="vertical")
    X_res = X_res.sort("index").drop("index")

    return X_res






3.2 Putting everything together in a Data Op






NoneLoading the file





The dataset is very large, so we downsample it to reduce the execution time. Note that we need to be deliberate with how we sample the data: rather than choosing a random subset of the values in the dataset, we need to be careful to select a subset of characters and keep all the rows for those characters. This ensures that we have reliable information about all the characters.

def sample_by_char(df, fraction=0.1):
    """
    Sample a fraction of chars and return all their data.
    """
    data = df.filter(
        pl.col("char").is_in(
            df.select(pl.col("char").unique())
            .sample(fraction=fraction, seed=42)["char"]
            .implode()
        )
    )
    return data


def load(file, fraction=0.1):
    if fraction == 1:
        print("Returning all users")
        return pl.scan_parquet(file)

    print(f"Sampling {fraction * 100}% of the users")
    df = pl.scan_parquet(file)
    df = sample_by_char(df.collect(), fraction=fraction)
    return df.lazy()










NoneFull Data Op construction script




# %%a
import skrub

def make_data_op():
    historical_data_file = skrub.var("historical_data_file")
    historical_data = historical_data_file.skb.apply_func(load)
    # In the guild column, null values are denoted by -1. This step replaces -1
    # with None. 
    historical_data = historical_data.with_columns(
        pl.when(pl.col("guild") == -1)
        .then(None)
        .otherwise(pl.col("guild"))
        .alias("guild")
    )

    user_month_has_played = historical_data.skb.apply_func(build_churn_dataset)
    X = user_month_has_played["char", "month"].skb.mark_as_X(cv=Splitter())
    y = user_month_has_played["has_played"].skb.mark_as_y()

    # Hyperparameters
    session_gap = skrub.choose_from([60], name="session_gap")
    use_location = skrub.choose_bool(name="location_features")
    add_gini = skrub.choose_bool(name="add_gini")

    all_features = X.skb.apply_func(
        add_features,
        historical_data.collect(),
        session_gap=session_gap,
        use_location=use_location,
        add_gini=add_gini
    )
    encoded = all_features.skb.apply(skrub.TableVectorizer())
    # data_op = encoded.skb.apply(SimpleImputer()).skb.apply(LogisticRegression(), y=y)
    data_op = encoded.skb.apply(
        HGB(learning_rate=skrub.choose_float(0.01, 1.0, log=True)), y=y
    )
    # data_op = encoded.skb.apply(DummyClassifier(), y=y)
    return data_op
